title: Jizo's Vow
speaker: Ryushin Andrea Thach
summary: The talk's main teaching is about finding balance and steadiness in life by invoking the support and protection of Jiso Bodhisattva, a Japanese figure associated with grief and protection, particularly for women and children. By embracing Jiso's fearlessness and flexibility, individuals can cultivate faith and trust that allows them to navigate uncertainty and chaos, even in the face of insurmountable problems. This teaching encourages listeners to find creative ways to honor and process their own experiences of pain and struggle, such as visiting a Jiso garden or making offerings, in order to find balance and steadiness in their lives.

sentences.text: Good evening, everyone.
It's really good to see everyone on this hot evening, and so many of you.
I was thinking, as I saw how full the zendo was, as full as I've seen it for a little while, how much we need the Dharma these days.
This talk kept rewriting itself today as I went about my activities, so we'll see how it turns out.
Many of you added to it this evening, too.
Tonight I want to talk about Jizo's vow.
How many of you know who Jizo Bodhisattva is?
Oh, quite a few of you.
I'm going to introduce you a little bit to Jizo and talk a little about what the vow is and why I see it as particularly important right now.
And then hopefully have a lot of room.
As the talk became clear to me, it became clear what the need might be in it, so we'll see what happens.
It seemed like a ripe time to talk about Jizo because, for the first time in Red Cedar's history, we did a Jizo ceremony here at Red Cedar earlier this month, I think.
Time's been really full.
The Jizo ceremony is typically performed in this country currently as a way of processing grief, particularly for children, and for children who have died.
I'll talk a little bit more about that.
A small group of us created a ceremonial space together and did the ceremony as it's come to us here through Yvonne Rand and Chozan Baez to this country.
I'll talk a little about that, too.
I think it was very powerful for the six people who were there to participate in it, and it will be the first of others.
Fair statement.
I also have been thinking a lot about the form of this ceremony and how it has come to us, for historical reasons, in a certain way.
But I see this as a time when there's a need for Jizo's vow and Jizo's presence.
Jizo Bodhisattva has been around since Buddha's time, or not long thereafter, and has made the trek from India to China and Japan.
But it's really his manifestation in Japan after World War II that we're most familiar with.
Can everyone hear me okay?
It's a little bit of a strain.
Maybe I can have you come here, because it's a little bit of a strain for my voice to come up anymore.
Whatever makes people feel comfortable.
Bring chairs up, or I'm not going to make it.
Come, come, come, come.
I don't bite.
You can get in front of someone.
You can be in this slot right here.
Move forward.
Okay.
After World War II was a very difficult time in Japan.
There was starvation.
People were very impoverished, and many women took the heartbreaking option of having abortions in order to be able to make it.
After a time it became clear that there was a lot of unresolved grief in that country, and so the priests made a ceremony having as its centerpiece Jizo.
That ceremony has been carried forward, so that Jizo has his embodiment in this country primarily in this form.
Jizo is usually depicted as a boy, as a child.
He's childlike.
He's open.
He's full of wonder and possibility.
He's also a monk.
He's a bodhisattva, a wisdom being, but he's a real person, unlike Avalokiteshvara and Manjushri and Maitreya, who are embodiments of a particular energy and are almost mythical in their proportion.
He's dressed as a humble monk, in the robe.
He's not usually found, in fact I don't think he's ever found, in a zendo routinely.
He is tonight because I brought a few of my little ones from home, and you can pass them around if you want.
In Japan, for those of you who have been, everywhere you go there are Jizos.
There are Jizos at three corners.
There are altars, boxes with Jizos inside, and usually there are many of them.
The cemeteries have many, many different Jizos.
Street corners, you can count on it.
People's homes too: at their home altar they may have a Jizo.
Jizo is traditionally dressed in his traveling clothes, and his traveling clothes are usually red, red being the color of the heart, of warmth, love.
Having looked at that, someone asked me the question, and that kind of confirmed my inclination.
He's dressed in robes, scarves, and capes, and bibs, kind of like rakusus or bibs like babies have.
People dress Jizo.

In fact, part of the ceremony that we have is that we sew traveling clothes for Jizo and offer them as a way of manifesting our grief and wishing well to the being who's either not present or whose journey we're assisting by our ceremony.
There are all kinds of Jizos.
I'm going to read you a short list.
Jizo is normally called the earth store, related to the earth.
He is called the Mizuko Jizo, or the water baby, a Jizo particularly for unborn children.
There's an [unclear: "asks for rain"] that helps the peasants in the field, helps warriors in difficulty and puts enemies to flight, leads horses and cattle.
There's a stomach wrapper Jizo who protects women during pregnancy.
There's a Jizo who protects houses and harvests from fire.
There's a Jizo who protects the miso, which is a staple food.
There's a Jizo that saves humans after death and leads them to enlightenment, that protects aborted fetuses, that takes the place of a woman so she can rest once a month.
There's the dream or sleep Jizo.
There's the Jizo you write letters to because [unclear: "it's death"].
And on and on and on.
There's a Jizo for every purpose.
The idea is that Jizo really is the protective spirit of those who are in need.
Originally, before this later incarnation in Japan, really for the poor, the downtrodden, the people who were in great difficulty and needed assistance.
That's who Jizo was, the wisdom saint for.
Typically he's depicted as carrying a staff with six rings.
He walks along, and the staff makes the sound of the six rings.
We actually use that staff in the mountain seat ceremony.
I think that's the main place we use that staff, also for certain Jizo ceremonies.
That staff has six rings, six rings for the six realms of existence.
We live in the human realm.
There's the deva realm.
There's the animal realm.
There's the fighting demon realm.
There's the hell realm, and on and on.
Jizo Bodhisattva is willing to travel in all of these realms.
He doesn't avoid any of them.
That's his vow.
He goes everywhere.
He's not afraid of the suffering.
In his other hand he carries the cintamani jewel.
The cintamani jewel is this radiant light.
It fulfills all wishes, all of the wishes of people who are making a request of him.
Traditionally people have made all kinds of requests of Jizo, for everything that we've read in the list and more.
This also is to light up the darkness in all of the hell realms that Jizo travels in.
The story of Jizo's vow is one that we can all relate to in some way.
It really arises out of the deep love a child has for her mother.
So the myth is that, historically, Jizo, or Kisitgarba Bodhisattva, was a Brahmin maiden, and her name was Sacred Girl.
She had a mother whom she loved dearly, as many daughters love their mother.
But the mother never accepted the Dharma.
Sacred Girl asked her and worried about her, and she never accepted the Dharma, and so she went to the hell realm.
Sacred Girl wouldn't let that happen to her mother, so she travels through all the hell realms in order to rescue her mother.
That's the story of how Sacred Girl became Jizo: because of the fervency of her wish, the depth of her compassion for her mother, and her fearlessness.
She becomes the embodiment of Jizo Bodhisattva.
Jizo then has two qualities primarily.
We invoke Kuan Yin or Avalokiteshvara for compassion.
We invoke Manjushri for wisdom.
We invoke Maitreya to become in touch with our Buddha nature, the Buddha that will become, which is all of us.
And Jizo has compassion and fearlessness, fearless compassion.
In July we studied the four methods of a Bodhisattva's guidance, but that's sometimes put as the three gifts of the Bodhisattva.
Do you know this?

The three gifts of the Bodhisattva, of those of us who are on the path, who are responding to the needs of the world, are material aid; giving the Dharma in whatever way; and the third one is fearlessness.
Fearlessness is the willingness to drop your self-centered ideas, your perspective, your judgments, your idea of what is, and just move to what's needed.
That's the gift of fearlessness.
Sacred Girl just knew her mother needed her, and she just went.
No thought of becoming anything or doing anything except responding to that need.
I think in part Jizo is a simple monk because he asks us to live our lives open and transparent, from a place of humble equality.
That's why he's out on the streets with everyone else.
That's why he's available to everyone.

Typically, Jizo Bodhisattva is meant to be involved for children with their miscarriages, abortions, for women, especially when they're pregnant, for travelers, for people in difficulty, and for animals.
My first experience of this ceremony was with Yvonne Rand at Green Gulch Farm, doing this ceremony for a child I chose not to have.
I never had questioned that it was the best decision, but that's never a good decision.

I've always dreamed of doing this ceremony for workers in animal shelters, for all the animals that have to be euthanized, for good, normal animals and the people who love them and carry that degree of suffering.
I think Jizo is very flexible.
We've already heard that.
These days, and this is where I'm getting ready to open it up to you guys, there's enormous suffering in the world.

All of us, sometimes quite consciously and sometimes not so consciously, are affected by the destruction of the planet and the effects of climate change that manifest in storms unimaginable, by violent speech and a climate that gives permission to that kind of violence, kind of unimaginable, people driving cars into people, and those who create a sense of uncertainty and fear.

We need Jizo Bodhisattva to help us find that center of fearlessness and that ability to stay open when we're frightened, to stay open when we're at odds, to stay open when our own anger, irritation, hatred, which arises from this uncertainty, arise and cloud our way of thinking.
I think Jizo Bodhisattva is really our Bodhisattva of this time because he's out in the streets with us.
He's living with us.
He's very flexible.
He can respond to whatever and be invoked for whatever.
There are many ways to honor Jizo.
There are easy little statues to find.
Like I say, I have a few in the back.
I have them scattered all over my house and in my garden.
There's a chant to evoke Jizo's vow that we can learn, that you can learn.
You can make your own little bib or your own little offering and put it on your altar.
But I think it's very important.
I was brought home to this not only by many conversations this evening, but today, a gift to this talk.
Someone came into the office to see me at work, where I take care of people.
Someone who said that he was suddenly not sleeping well.
It had been about two weeks.
Overwhelming anxiety, something he'd only experienced once before in his life.
The specifics and details are changed to protect the innocent, or details you can't guess.
Only once before, under a period of extreme duress, but the precipitant had been very clear.
So I asked, "What's happening this time?"
He didn't have a clue, actually.
Didn't have a clue why his mind was going like this all night long.
His heart was beating like this and he was just overwhelmed.
As we talked more, it became clear: well, there was Houston and all of those images of the people, and the memories of Katrina, and there was Charlottesville, and there's just the general background.
I won't call it noise.
I'll call it general background flavor.
If you've ever studied Buddhism from a Theravadan standpoint, we say that there's a feeling tone: how we perceive things is either pleasant, unpleasant, or neutral.
Usually it's pleasant or unpleasant.
And that feeling, when it's strong, pervades all of our perceptions.
All of our perceptions are pervaded right now by all of our experiences, and we feel it.
We're mammalian organisms.
We have a limbic system.
We're resonating with each other.
And for better or worse, we're all feeling what's happening.
So I think we need Jizo Bodhisattva to invoke a steadiness, to offer our grief to our sense of safety and security in the world that we all on some level feel in some way.
The paradigm just seems to be changing constantly.
Where can you point your direction in something that's stable?
It doesn't seem like it, too readily, right now.
Uncertainty is what's stable.
So how do you find your sense of balance?
So I want to open it up to everyone, because part of how we find our sense of balance is in our practice and in community.
This is one example of how we might.
Is anyone friends with Jizo Bodhisattva?
Has anyone invoked his name?
Has anyone found their grief spilling over without realizing it, and a way to live and move with it?
**Participant:** Yesterday I was going to meet someone I hadn't met before who was going to help me with a project.
I was interested in this opportunity.
As I was driving there, I was feeling like I was in this rattling crazy cage of our current conditions, and thinking how can I meet this person when I'm feeling all tossed around.
I did meet her and we talked and had a really good conversation, and it was like she could have been Jizo.
She brought something that I really wanted, even in this cage.
And it freed me from the cage.
So I am repeatedly amazed and grateful that time passes and new things, better things happen.
Without our making it, there actually is a lot of kindness and goodness too.
It's kind of like breathing through the racket until they appear.
Thank you.

**Participant:** I've been trying something that I forget if it was John or Bob, maybe someone, when we talked the last time, said that they had really been making a point of making eye contact and being really present to thank the cashier in the grocery line.
Or the person who, I don't know, I think that's mostly what has come up for me in that kind of exchange, of someone doing their job and me as the customer or whatever.
But it's really made a difference in how I feel throughout my day.
And it's been interesting, the reactions I've gotten, because sometimes it's a reaction of almost surprise or a slight lightening and a smile.
And I think it probably doesn't happen very often.
So I'm going to try to continue that practice.
I think that's really important these days.
**Participant:** Yes.
I never heard of Jizos until I went to Japan and was inundated with them in all forms.
Some of them really crude and even some of them very elegant.
One of the most stunning displays to me was in a cemetery where there were three tall Jizos and they were black.
And they were cradling these gold, like a cross section of a fetus.
So, you know, [unclear: "the blessing to the island"].
And earlier this year my daughter had to terminate a pregnancy because she learned that her baby had cystic fibrosis.
And I had occasion to be looking through my photographs and found that.
And held onto it for a little while because I didn't want to just throw it at her.
But the whole [unclear: "lot"] went by and one day I felt like, okay, I can send this to her now.
And she got back to me immediately and said that that very day, she's one of those people who everything is always okay.
She's really efficient.
She really takes care of a lot of stuff.
So it seemed like this was all just okay.
But she said that that very day that she got it, before she got it, she'd been getting her hair cut and everything came on her, just sitting there in the chair.
And then she came home and that was there.
**Ryushin Andrea Thach:** Please, yeah.
**Participant:** When I did the Jizo ceremony of the Chozen Roshi, it was a really unique experience, process, feeling the trauma that I'd never really given space to.
And that's what I really appreciate.
I was so grateful for the ceremony.
It was this trauma I'd so buried.
I had some more recent trauma.
I hadn't buried that.
I finally had space to really embody that and experience that safely.
It's something I don't think our own culture necessarily provides people.
Which is why I found that so valuable.
It's something we don't really give people space to do here.
And it's so valuable to have that.
Something I kind of took away from Japan, studying there, was the optimism, too.
That after [unclear: "baiting the faith that the bow was bound with us"], and we carry on anyway.
And that's something that helped me process Charlottesville and etc.
That we will never solve these problems, and they are unsurmountable.
And we carry on anyway, with that faith that this vow carries through.
Thank you very much for your teaching, Sharon.
We don't seem to get much attention, generally, in our teachings.
And it's interesting, this exception, that Jizo brings to mind.
**Ryushin Andrea Thach:** But yeah, there's a lot of animal suffering, too.
I think, in part, Jizo is so childlike.
Animals have that kind of innocence, too.
And so Jizo relates to animals.
And also, Jizo goes to the animal realm.
Although we all know that animals aren't actually the same kind of animals we are.
In fact, one of those Jizos back there was made special for me during a time I was at Tassajara by a woman who was a very skilled sculptress.
She was getting older when she made it.
But I left my then 16-year-old dog behind to go to Tassajara.
And I worried about her every day.
So I have a dog Jizo back there.
In fact, my teacher, who's very fond of dogs, also wanted one, as well.
You'll see that Jizo is usually depicted either holding a child, sometimes, or with children at the bottom of his robes, and also animals.
Kind of like Saint Augustine.
Saint Francis, thank you.
Like Saint Francis.
**Participant:** That brings up the story of one thing that happened to me on the beach in California.
I was grieving for my husband, who had died 14 years before, but we used to go to this beach a lot.
And I just really felt his presence.
And I was sitting in there and feeling really sad.
Also glad to be feeling sad about it.
And a big German shepherd came up and sat with me for the entire, you know, for about an hour.
I didn't know him.
He didn't know me, but he came over and just took care of me.
It was wonderful.
I didn't think of him as a Jizo.
**Ryushin Andrea Thach:** Obviously.
Obviously so.
**Participant:** I terminated the pregnancy 34 years ago.
And at that time, it was just pragmatic.
I just felt like this has to be done.
I did it.
Just moved on with my life.
I never really wanted to think about it, didn't think about it, didn't talk to anybody about it.
And I attended the Jizo ceremony here that we had two weeks ago.
And it was very powerful.
That had not come up for me until that ceremony allowed that death and that grief.
That I had been buried for 36 years.
And I was really wanting to, and I'll do this now, I really want to encourage, if we get a chance and we do it next year or whenever we do it again, I want to encourage everybody to come if you can.
It was very powerful for me in that sense.
I didn't have any expectation that that would happen.
So it was really quite moving.
I have to thank you, Andrea, for bringing that forward.
**Ryushin Andrea Thach:** Very much it's about creating a quiet container that can hold everything and then making an offering.
So when you think about this time and whatever it is, it's kind of in your front.
You become aware of it.
I think many people are becoming aware of the depth of their, it's not just superficially, I'm angry about this or I'm upset about this or how could so-and-so be doing this.
It's more a grief for a sense of, fill in the blank, security, safety, community, civility, kind of common ground that we have.
We each made our own offering, something to allow that to move along.
And then we made also little prayer flags, just strips of paper.
And we wrote on them our wish.
So we also make a wish.
Jizo has a cintamani jewel.
And we make that wish.
That helps us be aware of our own vow.
Our own vow to show up, to be kind, to look people in the face, to be an antidote to those emotions that roil around, that get stimulated by all that we're bombarded with.
Just one kindness.
Everyone's so hungry for it.
Everyone's so ready to receive and respond.
It's kind of like being in a desert and having a little bit of rain.
You can be that little bit of rain in some way, maybe.
I'm going to say, if many of you haven't seen it, the Jizos that we clothed in those prayer flags are out back in the gardens.
So please visit them.
And there's Jizo in the dark south room, too.
But these are the ones in the ceremony.
You're also welcome to make something without the ceremony.
If there's something that's on your mind you want to honor or think about, you can go to the Jizo garden at any point and make that offering.
That's also part of the practice.
So I think, oh, please.
**Participant:** I always felt that that ceremony wasn't really appropriate for me because I haven't lost a child.
But I've raised a child with special needs.
And in a way that's a series of deaths of many, many comings over many years of grief for what happened.
This can be children in distress.
I've had friends do this ceremony for children who are bipolar and in their 40s and 50s and suffering terribly.
Or for the parents.
The last time I did this I did the ceremony for my birth mother who never was able to resolve her grief and difficulty.
So you can be creative.
**Ryushin Andrea Thach:** Jizo allows you to be creative.
He's not restrictive.
You can do a ceremony to have good tasting miso too.
I think that's what we have time for unless there's anyone who's been holding back.
